items.heading: The Easter Holiday - Halls Green, Training Camp.
items.summary: Reg Hopkins' account of the boys' Easter training camp at Halls Green, listing the fourteen who went.
items.text:
Reg Hopkins reports:

This was the first of what I hope will become a regular feature for our younger members. Being the first, however, we naturally had teething troubles. A late start going was most disappointing and the cancellation of a proposed road relay on the homeward trip due to expected Bank holiday traffic conditions, that didn't materialise, was most unfortunate. And all, of course missed Mum's cooking !
Knowing now the possibilities of this place, and by planning our programme rather better, and making our own travelling arrangements we can eliminate those points that didn't favour us and spend an even better weekend next time.
All 14 Boys certainly did enjoy themselves. The weather, although not warm, did stay dry and allow us to spend most of the day out and about in the country. We spent one whole day canoeing on the river Medway (very tough on the arms - good for the throwers) and this was great fun for all, only one boy(who shall remain nameless) fell in. Having been told that rock climbing could be dangerous we gave that a miss, but we did have an enjoyable afternoon hill climbing. Ascending a steep hill with loose soil and very few handholds took quite a lot of strength and determination and was pretty hard on the seat of one's pants coming down. Among other activities we enjoyed were high jump and javelin contests. We also had weight training sessions every day and these proved most popular. I think, however, that the most popular pastime was throwing Nigel Bacon in the swimming pool !
We played some good games of football too (we have quite a good team - how about a match you seniors?)
The funniest occurance throughout the weekend, apart from Nigel being chased "Starkers" through the countryside, was being confronted by the bigest Great Dane we have ever seen, during a cross country run. All put on a brave front and tried to frighten it away but the look of terror on our faces was hilarious.
As we had planned, we showed some movie films, including Belgrave's own classic; this the boys loved and it certainly increased their pride in being "Bels Boys".
Tom Carter and Tony Brooks paid us a visit on the Saturday. It was a great pleasure to all when they arrived just in time to give lifts back to the camp; we had been on the return march of an 8 mile cross country ramble and still had some way to go.
All in all it was a good weekend and I am already planning the next one.
To conclude, I would very much like to pass on some comments from various people outside the club regarding the behaviour of our lads. For example, "what a friendly and cheerful crowd they all were" and "how willing to share the chores that had to be done". Well done lads, we are proud of you.
Those who went.
Nigel Bacon, Reg Hopkins, Tony Lloyd, Vic Butcher, Ian McNally, Stephen Corrigan, Bill Curtin, Mark Waight, John Clements, Richard Langley, Chris McKeavor, John Hickey, Martin Bloice, Mick Harvey. Sooty.

May 21st--Crystal Palace
We had 16 of our Club members taking part in this schools meeting, which was the first to be held on the already famous "Tartan" track.
Most outstanding were Steve White in the 200 metres and Arnold Bent in the High Jump and Bill Curtin winning the 800 metres once again.
Steve looked terrific, and who can say where this fellow will advance in the world of sprinting.
Arnold injured himself on the last of his jumps otherwise he would have most certainly improved even more than the new personal and championship best that he gained.
Bill, showing all the ability he has displayed so often, attacked in the finishing straight and broke his opponents completely.
A word about young Reg Hopkins. Still only a second year boy, he won his place in his school team by proving beforehand that he is better than any 3rd or 4th year pupil at his school. He has, therefore, two more years in this same race and hopes that he will follow in the footsteps of his idol Bill Curtin and be a future winner.

items.heading: Camberley and District Young Athletes Meeting Bracknell Berks.
items.summary: Reg Hopkins reports the Camberley and District young athletes meeting at Bracknell on 3 June 1968, where eight Belgrave boys won six medals and Richard Langley set a boys' half-mile record (continued on page 24).
items.text:
Monday---June 3rd
REG HOPKINS WRITES:--
8 Boys went along to this all day meeting and I am delighted to say we met with great success. This without doubt is a meeting of a very high standard, and so coming away with 6 medals, with so small a team,was a grand effort.
But through some bad luck--Bill Curtin being injured (although he did come along and give the boys his support) and a thunderstorm just before the start of the 100 yds--we might well have had two more winners.
Our principal victory was Richard Langley's winning of the boys half mile in a new record time (previously held by none other than our own Bill Curtin). He won in a most impressive way and looked every inch a champion--what a great prospect we have in this youngster---and his winning time of 2:09.9 will only be a personal best for a very short time I know. He took 2.3 off Bill's best of last year and we all know this must be a feat in itself. He also took the Cup.
The next thing to please us was Barry Quirk's 2nd place in the 80 metres Hurdles where he shared the same time as the winner (12.0). How the judges managed to split them I don't know. He started without blocks, allowing the other boy a couple of yards on him up to the first Hurdle but from there on he was moving faster, and had the race been half a yard longer he must have won.
The race that gave me greatest pleasure was the 4x110 yd Relay. In spite of our team having only the briefest baton changing practice (this is going to be rectified) the boys won themselves 3rd place medals. Martin Bloice was moving with tremendous speed on his leg, and indicated that had the weather not changed just before his heat of the 100 yds, which unsettled him a great deal, his entry into the final would have been almost certain; likewise his chance for a medal.
Another of our boys who won fame for himself was Vic Butcher. Although only placing 4th in the 1000 metres steeplechase (his first ever) he gained for himself A.A.A. 2nd Class standard with a time of 3min:8secs--no mean feat. Mick Harvey also ran in this race and was only fractionally outside A.A.A. 3rd Class standard of 3min:25secs. What is important for him, however, is that he has at last proved to himself that he can do it--now watch out all you other blokes.
David Wilkinson had his first outing for some time; having just returned from Germany where he has been living since last summer. Finishing fourth in the Javelin with a personal best throw of 139ft-5" delighted him and now he is looking for some expert coaching to improve still more. Another of our throwers, Jimmy Paraskeva, had personal bests of 100ft-7" (Javelin) and 85ft-1" (Discus) to his credit.
(Cont'd on page 24)

(Cont'd from page 40)
Reg Hopkins had a successful day with a 2:28 half mile on a well churned up track and by helping the relay team to its 3rd place--not bad for a 13 years old !
A word of thanks to Nigel Bacon who was too old to run at this meeting; this did not stop him from breaking into his holiday and coming all the way from Brighton to cheer us on in his own inimitable way. This is the spirit that is going to make our boys the best in the country before long.
Also,a word of thanks to the parents who made the trip to see our team perform. I wish more would follow their example. It is a terrific stimulus to us all.to see and hear them in the stands.

We at Golden Wonder would like to change things. We'd like to see a British winner on that proud rostrum in Mexico. We'd like to see lots of them. British athletes in the past have been unable to match the state-sponsored supermen from the Iron Curtain. Or from the States. And with Mexico's dizzy altitude things are going to be even tougher. We've already donated £3,000 for high altitude training in the Pyrenees. You can help us donate a lot more. And win yourself a trip to Mexico to see it all happening.

How you can get to Mexico...
Five prizes of two weeks for two people at the Olympic Games. That'll be our Golden Award to you for helping Britain's Olympic effort. Just look at the questions on the right and send your answers to us together with your empty Golden Wonder packs. We promise to donate 2d. to the British Amateur Athletic Board for every five empty Golden Wonder Crisp packets we receive; for every one Golden Wonder Nuts packet we receive, we'll donate 1d.* And remembering that over 40 million packets of crisps are sold in Britain every week, we could, between us, go a long way towards helping Britain strike gold.

items.heading: POSTBAG
items.summary: Postbag column with news of walker John Knifton in New York, Harry Shields' letter criticising the Byers Report and the trade-name ruling, and Chris Steer's farewell before leaving for Canada.
items.text:
JOHN KNIFTON, one of our leading walkers a few years back, has been in the U.S.A now for three years--- and he is still in the heel and toe game. Not just, but to the tune of a 92:46 20 Kilos! The occasion was the annual Nat Osk Memorial 20 Kilos in New York's Central Park and, of the 52 competitors, John finished third behind two top American walkers, Dave Romansky (90:04) and Ray Somers (91:35). His 4 minutes allowance enabled him to take the handicap award. John, who works at the Texaco Oil Company's Research Centre, writes "I am presently training five times a week but have changed my schedule. I no longer bother with strolling, instead I've reverted to strip training spins of 15-20 miles twice a week. This type of training gives, I feel, increased strength without jeopardising speed". A foot injury in the week preceding the American National 25 Kilos race upset his preparation, but he still finished 10th in 2:05:32 over a measured course (Ron Laird, the U.S.A.'s No.1 was 3rd). By the birth of his son, Matthew, last December John made former Belgravian Editor BEN KNIFTON a proud grandfather.

The article in the March BELGRAVIAN entitled "Remove the Shackles" has galvanised Past President HARRY SHIELDS into literary action. Harry has been right through the mill of club athletics and no one is ever likely to match his achievement of gaining a team-winners medal in the National Cross-Country Championship and the National Race Walking Championship. He knows what makes clubs tick and, like many others, is sceptical of the Byers Report. He writes"The Byers Report suggests the cure to the malaise to be lots of money and an omnipotent overlord. The Sunday Telegraph suggests that a strong candidate is John Disley and quote no less a sponsorship than the International Athletes"Club" and in particular Peter Hildreth, Chris Brasher and Derek Johnson. How on earth these qualify to give opinions I do not know------while the good they have done (in voluntary work) compared with our own officials is beyond me".
Harry continues "The need for a centralised administration combining the work of the AAA, BAAB and WAAA etc. has long been appreciated but I have yet to read of any understanding of club organisation. In due time it appears to me that the chasm between the A.A.A.'s administration and clubs like our own will be so wide as not to require each other".
Harry mentions that for many years he has been a "hanger-on" to that band of voluntary workers who organise our top athletic meetings, and he wonders "how the gaps will be bridged between the professional administration at the top, club organisation and the body of people at present prepared to turn out in all weathers, using their extensive knowledge without recompense".
He adds a tail-piece on that hysterical ruling regarding trade names on hold-alls. "I have reached the exalted position of 'Chief Blanker Out'. What a lot of nonsense it is, particularly when you think of the Stadium being full of 'Pepsi-Cola', 'News of the World' and other adverts on which the television cameras are constantly trained. This does not seem to offend the aesthetic sense of Don Pain and the Marquess".
Harry always was a bit of a rebel---The I.A.A.F. and Lord Byers should keep him going for some time!.

CHRIS STEER wrote the day before he left for Canada and sends best wishes to all his 'mates' in the Club. Rivals of Steer cannot afford to ease up, for he says"I shall be taking my running kit with me to keep my hand---or should I say foot-in". He continues "I'll keep in touch with the Club of course (I've even paid my subs) and perhaps a 'letter from America' column à la Alistaire Cooke will be appropriate".
It will be interesting to see by how much Chris swells our Postbag column in future editions.

items.heading: Stop Press! KINNAIRD TROPHY RESULT
items.summary: Stop-press result of the Kinnaird Trophy, where Belgrave were sixth of ten clubs in their first year back, with a John Thresher 1500m win.
items.text:
Belgrave can feel well pleased with this result. Polytechnic invite the ten clubs they consider to be the strongest in the land and this was our first year back in. Birchfield, Achilles and Poly were always reckoned to be out of reach but the points score shows that not much extra was needed to get in amongst these teams. After all, if Derek Boosey and Arnold Bent had been available our points score would very likely have been boosted to 36 or 37---by such margins are these trophies won or lost. Full strength teams are absolutely vital for the forthcoming National League matches.
John Thresher had one of the easiest wins of the afternoon, taking the 1500 metres by a 3 seconds margin in 3:46.2---equivalent to a 4min-4sec mile. The heat was oppressive and Bill Kerr, running at the worst time of all, showed magnificent fighting qualities in the 5000 metres. He finished 4th in 14:36.2, 14.2 seconds behind P. Stewart (Birchfield). What team spirit by Laurie O'Hara! Having done his day's training, and all set for an afternoon's spectating, he was roped in for the 5,000 metres and finished 9th of the 17 runners.
Nick Head did season's bests in Javelin and Shot, as did Tony Brooks in his heat of the 800 metres. Jim Vivian finished 5th in the 200 metres final and John Dear 4th in steeplechase (9:51.6).
